utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in the court. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today we are Wednesday. I'd like to greet Mr. Scott, Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the people present in the courtroom. We shall resume the cross-examination of the witness. Prior to that, I will give the floor to the registrar who has a few IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The OTP has submitted its response to Exhibits tendered by accused Praljak for Witness DW. This list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 689. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As far as time allocation is concerned, for Defence counsel, Mr. Prlic has an hour with an additional 30 minutes which was given to him by Mr. Pusic, which amounts to 1 hour and 30 minutes. So far 47 minutes have already been taken up, unless somebody has given him more time. But for the time being, it is an hour and a half. Is that correct, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, it is not, Mr. President. I believe the Pusic time has been given to Ms. Senka Nozica. I have, as I indicated to the registrar, I have a half an hour from the Petkovic team, a half an hour from the Praljak team, and I understand approximately 15 minutes from the Coric team. So I anticipate spending the rest of the first session on my feet doing cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, everyone in and around the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's pick up where we left off yesterday; and I believe, at the end of the day, we were talking about non-residential accounts. You had confirmed to us that there was nothing illegal or nefarious about having such accounts, and so I want to just go through a couple more documents to close this chapter. We'll see perhaps how these residential accounts were used in some ways, these non-residential accounts. If we can look at 1D 01763, 1763. It should be in your packet, and this is dated November 9, 1992. We see that it's a letter from the public company for production, transmission, and distribution of electric power, Elektroprivreda. Have you found it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May we have some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're going to have to work with me, sir, because I have a limited amount of time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So let's get with it. Now, if we look at this document - please look at it for a second - you'll see that it was generated from Sarajevo from the director general of the Elektroprivreda company. And in the subject, it says, "Provision of means in foreign currency." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we just -- and I'm just going to walk you through parts of it. I just want you to confirm this. You may not have personal knowledge, but this is part of the process. On the very first sentence, it starts with: "As you already know, a certain time ago the business premises of Elektroprivreda BiH public company was completely burned down as a consequence of wartime activities of the aggressors." I take it when they're speaking of the aggressors at this point in time, in 1992, November 9, in Sarajevo, they must be speaking about what was commonly referred to back then - not that I subscribe to the term - but what some people call the Chetniks or the Serb forces or the former JNA. Is that what we're talking about when we say "aggressors" here?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go to the second paragraph, it talks and says: "With the aim of regaining control over electro-energetic system and creating of better performance conditions, Elektroprivreda BiH decided to procure four satellite telephones," and then later on you'll see, in the same paragraph, that they're going to be procured from a company called Hetring, and the amount is approximately $239.000 US. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we go into the next paragraph, it talks about: "Since the electric power is delivered abroad by Elektroprivreda ... only to Croatia, we do not possess convertible currency." Now, I take it one of the reasons there is no convertible currency is because at this point in time, as you had indicated yesterday, the central bank was not functioning and the banking system was not functioning in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say, in the next paragraph: "With the aim of solving this problem," that is, the procurement of foreign currency for satellite telephones," we propose that these means from the foreign currency account of the Armed Forces of the Republic of BiH are paid to our account, and that Elektroprivreda of BiH for that purpose puts at disposal of the Armed Forces of BiH its claim from the Republic of Croatia in Croatian dinars at the official exchange rate." Let's park here a little bit. They're talking about a foreign currency account of the armed forces of BiH. So, obviously, it would appear, at least, whoever is generating this document, which happens to be the general director -- the director general of Elektroprivreda, he's aware of a foreign currency account of the forces of BiH. Where would that be? Would you know? Would that be in Sarajevo or would that be outside in some other -- in some non-residential account, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This account or one of the accounts that the BH army had was, for instance, opened in Austria, but probably it had another in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So, in other words, what you're telling us is that the -- the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or its armed forces had -- had accounts outside the country, non-residential accounts as well?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Now I have to go back, with your permission, to my case where we were accused of illegally spending resources from the Republic of Croatia. As you saw in the balance sheet, final balance sheet, every kuna which came from the Republic of Croatia has its written trace, where it was spent; whereas, with the BH army, and we provided this to the Prosecution, Mr. McNair, a list of documents where Mr. Alija Izetbegovic on a piece of paper would write, for instance, give Haris Silajdzic, Hasan Cengic, and others a million dollars, for instance. And with that piece of paper, handwritten, he goes to Vienna and picks up a million dollars without any trace of where he spent it or they spent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, I believe that there is some documentation that was provided to the Office of the Prosecution, with respect to those secret bank accounts that Mr. Silajdzic and others had access to, though they chose not to indict those individuals, but that's another story. Let's focus on this. If we look at the next document, 1D 01767, 1767, here we see -- if we can find it real quickly. While you're looking for it, it was generated January 26, 1993. It's signed by a Zlatko Lagumdzija. Do you know of this individual? Do you know of him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him personally, but I do know that he was president of the SDP of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And here he signed this document as vice-president of the government of RBiH, January 26, 1993, and here we have a decision on opening of non-residential dinar and foreign currency account in the Republic of Croatia. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And, again, this document would confirm, would it not, that non-residential accounts are being opened by the government of BiH?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at III, it says: "The accounts that are not opened in the Republic of Croatia, in line with the provisions of this Decision, shall not be considered to be the accounts of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, I don't know how it's -- how you read it, but correct me if I'm wrong or assist us. Would this imply, if I read it correctly, that through this decision, they're designating a non-residential account for the Republic of BiH, but they're not excluding the opening of non-residential accounts for others; but simply that, unless the account is opened pursuant to this particular decision, it cannot be considered, one, to be that of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Am I correct in reading it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, but it means that they had opened accounts beforehand, previously, and they were forced to align those accounts with the decision to make them valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, one last document, and this is P 00985. This is a Prosecution document. I think you might have it. You should have it in your bundle. No, you don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I need the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to give it to you right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document, incidentally, for the record, came from the Prosecution motion for admission of documentary evidence, dated 20 September 2007, to which the Defence has been granted leave to file its response, I believe it's 18 November 2007 -- October, I'm sorry, 18 October 2007. So that's where this document came. It hasn't been translated by the Prosecution. We translated the first -- the first page, and it might be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could just look at that, it's dated 1 October 2003. It's from the Privredna Bank Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I just want to read part of this and it's been highlighted for you, the section that I want to look at it. I want to go on the record, read it, and maybe you can help had us out here. It says here: "Subject: Response to the decision, operational number XXXKIR 3077/03. "Having inspected and analysed the contents of decisions, taking into consideration the legal regulations, we respond as follows: From the request, one can conclude that the interest is directed to persons related to activities of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which we were given non-residential accounts in the Republic of Croatia, in the banks authorised for affairs with foreign countries, in their field offices most suitable and closest to BiH borders. "The basis for opening those accounts was the agreement of payments between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina signed on 19th of March, 1992, as well as the instruction of MFRH," that must be Ministry of Finance Republic of Croatia, "dated 5th of May, 1992, that explained to the banks the way of running business with BiH, and that requested immediate activities in order to reduce the consequences of payment circulation, suspension, and other communications caused by war in this area."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm told that what is on the e-court right now is not the one that's been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, having looked at this, can you comment at all? What exactly are we learning from this particular document dated 2003?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this, we can conclude that the investigating judge established that everything had been done contrary [as interpreted] to the law, referring to agreements between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 19th of March, 1992, and the guidelines from the Ministry of Finance of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the translation, it says "contrary to the law." That would mean against the law, or is it in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, let me go back and look at this document again. According to the transcript, it says here that what you're saying is that this was a crime. A crime was being -- this document shows that a crime was being committed. My reading of it is that everything is done consistent with agreements between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I realise that counsel has indicated that this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought it was on. My apologise. Your Honour. I understand that Mr. Karnavas says this document has come from the Prosecution, and it's not fully translated. Be that as it may, we're at a complete loss to be able to follow this testimony and be able to look at the document. We have nothing in front of us which allows us to follow this testimony or to study the document, and it's impossible. And given the dispute that's going on with the which is now, it's impossible for us to know what's happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise to my colleague Mr. Karnavas. But as we can follow better whether the interpretation was correct, I'd like to say that in line 8 -- line 17, "contrary" is not the proper interpretation of what the witness said. He said it was "in keeping with" and not "contrary." So it's "in keeping with," and that Mr. Karnavas' attempt to put that right was fully in order. He thought he was being asked about crime. Anyway, there was may have understanding between Mr. Karnavas and the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I was trying to say, that there was a misinterpretation. So it is confirmation that everything is done in keeping with the agreement and with the guidelines issued by the Ministry of Finance. So there was absolutely nothing wrong there. Had there been any other acts contrary to anything like this, then that would probably be a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes, she apologises, but she heard "suprotno" and not "sukladno," and that's where the mistake came from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I appreciate the clarification from Ms. Alaburic, but our point remains the same. We just simply have no ability to follow this testimony without having the translation of the document. I don't know the entire context of what's been said. I can't follow the testimony, and it would be helpful if we would have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could be of assistance, that's all I needed to get out of the document. Secondly, Mr. President, we expect that this entire document will be translated. We also expect that we will be answering to this document when we make our submissions on 18 October 2007, because, as I noted, this came from the Prosecution motion for admission of documentary evidence, which also begs the question that should be asked perhaps by the Trial Chamber to the Prosecution, how dare they submit documents of which they don't even know what's inside and attempt to get them in before the Trial Chamber for this Court's consideration. One would assume, with the thousands and thousands and thousands of documents that we have, they would at least do some screening and know which of those documents are necessary and relevant to the case. So, therefore, I must say, with all due respect to my colleague who I know is overburdened, just as I am, that he ought to know what's in his documents and should not leave it up to me, another foreigner, to try to figure out through my staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, that's not -- that's not a fair comment, but, as usual, it's the sort of thing that the Prosecution comes to expect from Mr. Karnavas. Of course, we don't contest the document apparently came from a Prosecution bundle. The Chamber well knows the limitations on this institution in terms of translation resources that we all suffer from. The Prosecution had done a partial translation, to date, so far of the parts that we were tendering into evidence. Now, whether the entire document will ultimately translated or not is a separate matter. But that is -- whether that needs to be done is a separate question from when we come into the courtroom with the witness where the exhibit is going to be used in court with the witness, that everyone in the courtroom needs to be able to follow the testimony. It's impossible for the Prosecution to have -- know what's being said without having the document in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, may I raise a point, because Your Honour knows the way we work on the Defence side and we are now faced with the response to this motion involving 539 documents. I'm the very lucky person who has the carriage of the particular drafting of this response. We share up the work. As I go through, if it's being dealt with in this way on the Prosecution's side, with partial translations not identified in the list of 539 documents, what am I supposed to do? Am I supposed to go to the Croatian version of the document, a language that I frankly don't understand, I can see the scale of the document, and be double-checking all the time to see whether the Prosecution have or haven't arranged a complete translation before they've whacked another 500 plus documents on us, in addition to the thousands we already have. It's just a practical matter, Your Honour. The whole thing is getting completely out of hand. May we know how they propose to deal with that aspect of the matter. I'm sorry for interrupting here, but it's linked to what Mr. Karnavas has been saying and it's linked to the particular practical problem which has arisen at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I should add, Mr. President, in all fairness to the Defence, and perhaps Mr. Scott is unaware of this, we did make a request to the Prosecution to have this document translated. This was done a few days ago, so we did attempt. First of all, they were on notice that this was a document that we intended to use with this witness, or they should have known that. They knew that there was a request by us. They failed to -- to translate it. So now to stand up and to cry a river over how, once again, they're being attacked by this -- this particular Defence attorney, I find it rather charming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, this document -- this document is not contained in the bundle. The document you've just used is seemingly not part of the bundle. When Defence counsel gives us a document or gives us a bundle of documents before the cross-examination, I leaf through all the exhibits to see how you intend to deal with your cross-examination; and if I realise that a translation is missing, then I step in and say that a translation is missing. But in this case, the document you've just used is not a document which I have in my possession. So I could not be aware of the fact that the translation was missing. Now, when there is a translation issue, the Trial Chamber feels the best way of dealing with this is to ask the attorney or Defence counsel to read the text in his or her own native language, and then the interpreters will translate it so that everybody can understand what's being read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I should note, and I stand -- you know, I totally accept your comments. As I indicated, we had made the request. The translation wasn't done. We had anticipated the Prosecution to perhaps be able to translate this document on short notice. They were not; hence, my improvisation. But in event, we'll move on. But we will get it translated for everyone's convenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to move on to another topic, and this topic deals with municipalities. Okay. It's a general topic, but I'm going to go through various documents from various municipalities. It's only a sampling of various issues, but it's a sampling for the Trial Chamber to understand part of your testimony. Because as I heard you correctly, you indicated that a lot of things were happening at the municipal level and that, in fact, you witnessed folks coming in from the various municipalities. Presidents of the municipalities were coming in and having private conversations with Mr. Mate Boban of which, of course, you were not a participant, but merely you saw them coming, and then they would make some decisions were apparently made. We'll leave it up to the Trial Chamber what to make of that, but --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. What you do mean by private conversations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, what I mean was that Mr. Boban was having conversations to these individuals; private, in the sense, that you weren't present at the time. These were conversations that he was holding, official conversations; private, in the sense, you were not a participant of.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the essential point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were official conversations but I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so the record is clear then, the entire -- the entire content of the witness's evidence on that is he saw people entering and leaving the building, and that's the -- he wasn't in the meetings. He can't say what happened in the meetings. So what the witness has just told us is he saw people coming into the building and going out of the building. That's the only evidence that he's given us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, you know, I don't want to turn this into a debating society. The gentleman, yesterday, indicated that presidents of municipalities would come and meet with Mate Boban, and then afterwards orders were issued with respect to the distribution of monies. That's what the gentleman indicated. This whole context came when the Prosecutor was trying to impeach the very same witness that he had, even though there were no grounds for it, but he made allegations that the witness was confabulating. Now, this was my -- that little introduction was just a segue into this particular chapter, because I'm dealing with various issues with respect to municipalities, so I was just cuing everybody in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right, Mr. Karnavas. Put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at document 1D 01772, this is a decision from the municipality of Tomislavgrad. 1772. All you've got to do is look at the yellow tab, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You're going to have to work with me quicker. I don't mean to pressure you, but we have limited time here. This is August 20, 1992, and here it says, this is a decision: "I am financing the needs of national defence." And in Article 1, it says: "With the aim of financing the defence in the territory of Tomislavgrad municipality, the contribution for defence shall be introduced." And then, in Article 2, we see that at that talks about citizens who have a salary, a domestic salary; and then, further down, you see that there is a breakdown: Citizens employed abroad have to pay 400 DM per passport. That's for men. Women have to pay a hundred, and then you have citizens employed in Austria. They pay a different amount. You see all of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So when you were talking about the municipalities self-financing their -- their defence, this is -- this is a document that assesses to that, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at -- if we look at the preamble, we see that it sets out that this is something that is being -- a decision that is being taken by the municipality of Tomislavgrad in accordance with their particular Statute; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we'll go on to the next document, and this is 1D 01771. 1771. This is May 2, 1992. And if we go to the preamble, we see that it is from the municipality of, or even at the very top, it says "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Assembly of Posusje." My apologies for the pronunciation. We see here this is a decision on obligatory financing of defence; again, another municipality. Article 1, it says: "The obligatory financing of municipality defence is introduced for all citizens from," and I underscore that word, "from the territory..." And then if you look at II, it talks about citizens "from the territory who are permanently employed abroad." So it seems that citizens from this municipality, as we have seen from Tomislavgrad, who are living abroad still have to make contributions to the war effort; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 01757, 1757, that is different kind of a document. We're going to deal with two documents from this particular municipality. This is from Orasje municipality, dated April 21, 1992. Here, in this decision, it says: This is from the War Presidency of this particular municipality, and it's a decision on conversion of, I guess, Yugoslav dinars from the treasury of domestic payment office from Orasje into Croatian dinars. Now, I take it -- and if we look at Article I, it says: "Hereby, the obligation of conversion of Yugoslav dinars from the Treasury of Domestic Payment Agency Office in Orasje into Croatian dinars is introduced." I take it that this was a necessary -- this was necessary in light of what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, vis-a-vis the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now let's look at the next document, 1758.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, this is just to give the Court a sampling of what's happening at the municipal level because of the concept of self-management, as it will become obvious throughout the course of this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a document dated September 19, 1992. It's a decision on establishing the right to financial compensation for families of fallen or missing soldiers of 106th HVO Brigade Bosanska Posavina. Now, yesterday, if I heard you correctly, you had indicated that payments about going to families of fallen soldiers. Correct? That was one of the obligations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And here is a good example, at least at the municipal level, where the municipality is trying to take care of the families of those who are protecting the homeland, based on the Territorial Defence that existed, at least at that point in time, and this is September 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That's -- we'll go on to the next document, and now we're going to talk about Mostar. Two documents. The first one will be 1D 01760. 1760. If we look at this, it starts with "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council, Mostar municipality," dated 25 -- July 25, 1992. This is a decision on "amendment to the decision on introduction of the Croatian dinar as the means of cash payment."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I just want to give the Trial Chamber an opportunity to see what's happening in various municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here we see in Article 1 that there is an amendment, and you will awe see the quotation parted, which says: "All participants in cash transactions are obliged to form the prices and state them in Croatian or Yugoslav dinars."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, here, they're given an opportunity -- they're saying that you have to designate two different currencies, one of either; that is, Croatian or Yugoslav dinars. Again, is this the kind of decision that would have been necessary in light of the financial situation - the monetary situation, I should say - in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So was it -- perhaps you may not be able to answer this question, but this is not an attempt to sort of Croatise - this is the kind of word we've heard bandied about - to Croatise the Mostar municipality by introduced a decision like this, but, rather, this would be a decision necessary, given that you need a currency that's viable in order to do certain transactions on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two reasons for this kind of a decision. The first basic reason was the fact that all trade - well, not all trade, but most of the trade - involved companies from the Republic of Croatia because payments were easier. The second reason is that, in the treasury of Yugoslavia, an enormous amount of Yugoslav dinars stayed behind, and they were brought into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is to say that the property of Bosnia-Herzegovina was purchased, devalued, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, if we look at the next document, 1D 1759, 1759, again, this is from the -- this is a decision: "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council, Mostar Municipality," and it's a decision on "war tax for workers for Mostar municipality territory working abroad, and retired persons who went into retirement after working abroad." And here we see, again, this would seem somewhat similar to the other documents from the other municipalities. At least, in Article 2, we see there is a tax, a war tax of 300 DEM. What does "DEM" mean, per month?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means 300 German deutschemark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need it for the record. And then we go into article 4, for instance, and it says: "The war tax shall be paid through transfer accounts," and we see Splitska Banka is one, "or in cash on the counter of the Office for Finances of HVO- Mostar municipality." So, here, it would appear that as of this date, September 16th, they're saying, Here is an account a non-residential account in Splitska Banka, and you can deposit it over there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's it for Mostar. If we go on to the next set of documents, the next municipality is going to be Livno, and it's a motley group of decisions that I'm going to go through. We're going to start off with 1D 01761. 1D 01761. Again, it says here, "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Livno municipality HVO," 26 March 1993: "Decision on financing of Livno HVO-sanctioning military conscripts." And if we look at that, we see that, at the very beginning, in Article I, it says: "Military conscripts who are temporarily working abroad with visas obtained before October 1991, and who upon their return to the municipality, their permanent residence, "did not report within eight days to the Livno OHVO Defence office to be mobilised to the Livno HVO units, shall finance the OHVO" the defence of Livno, "by paying 900 German marks a month from the moment they failed..." In other words, they are being punished, to some extent, for failing to report to duty. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that's all we need for this document. We'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to give the Court again an indication what's happening at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next document is 1D 0308, 308. This is a decision of 2 April 1993, and, again, we can see it's the "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Livno municipality, Croatian Defence Council." This is a decision on financing of Livno OHVO sanctioning military conscripts. It's somewhat similar to the previous one, and we can -- would you agree, if you just look at Article I, that this is something similar to the first one that we just looked at, the difference being the date and there's some minor differences on who this was forwarded to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, if we go on to the next document, 3 -- 1D 00307, 307. This is dated 16 April 1993. This is a decision on assignment of financial aid to the Bruno Busic HVO Regiment. And if we look at Article I, it says that "the Bruno Busic HVO Regiment is hereby assigned financial aid in the amount of 1.500.000 Croatian dinars." And it says here, in Article II: "The finances office of the municipal HVO shall withdraw cash from the Livno municipal HVO cashier."" Now, from this document, can we conclude that Livno is financing, through this decision, this professional -- this brigade or this regiment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Helping.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And this had a professional brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to take the floor because this document is quite disturbing. It proves that this Bruno Busic Battalion was funded under municipality decisions, because a certain amount is earmarked for this battalion. We're on the 5th of April, 1993. As far as you know -- I'm not sure you will be able to answer. You might not be the appropriate witness to answer that question. But since you have been in charge of such duties, you may be privy to that. Budget-wise, the funding of a regiment, is it not the role of the Minister of Defence, could you explain that to me, and not the municipality. Could you explain that to me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I corrected the attorney. It is not financing. This is just a one-off thing, assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that it is assistance. It is support. We're not talking about funding, because as a rule in regiments the salaries have to be approved by the Ministry of Defence and go through the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, but there were other expenses involved as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So your answer to my question seems to be that, in this case, we're talking about some type of support. Yes, I can see "support" in English. Very well. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just to -- so the amount, again, seems rather -- let's see, it's 1.500.000 Croatian dinars. How much is that are we talking in deutschemarks?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say between 2 and 3.000 German marks; around 2.000 deutschemark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's what it would have been at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go on to the next document, this is 1D 01762, 1762. This is September 24, 1993. This is -- here, we see it's "the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Municipal HVO Livno." So, here, at this point in time, we're dealing with the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is a decision on "professionalisation of the army within the HVO Brigade, Petar Kresimir IV, and defining of adequate salaries." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we look at Article II, it says: "The special salary adequate to TIP for members of the professional units of the brigade Petar Kresimir IV HVO Livno is defined, as of September 1, 1993." Can you comment on this? Why was it necessary to have a decision of this nature passed by the Livno municipality on the 24th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard now to remember why exactly. Well, quite simply, probably, this had become quite a burden for the municipality, this financing. That could have been one of the reasons. And another reason was that by then the HVO was slowly being established as an army, which, I mean, well, should have as many professional soldiers as possible, and that the Home Guard's part should be reduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say the "Home Guard," are we talking about based on the Territorial Defence, the concept of All People's Defence and then the Territorial Defence? Is that what you're talking about when you say "Home Guard"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Herceg-Bosna, we no longer had a Territorial Defence. We had the Domobrani Home Guard. That is a Croatian expression for the same form of unit. Well, I cannot say form of unit but I cannot say people, but same formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I take it those formations were drawn from the particular municipalities, for the municipalities, by the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Like in the former Yugoslavia, there was the Territorial Defence. It was municipal. So the Domobrani regiments, or rather, the Domobrani, the Home Guards were people from the local territory of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the next document, that's 1D 00297 and this is the last document for Livno. This is October 9 1993. This is the decision on the "amount of compensation, daily allowance for private sent on assignment pursuant to an order issued by the HR HB HVO Main Staff." Here, it says a decision was passed for compensation of 17 deutschemarks per day payable. Do you see that sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It seems this has to do with the Petar Kresimir IV HVO Brigade. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Home Guard unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Okay. So now we know what was happening in Livno a little bit. Now I want to focus on a set of documents and -- for the Tuzla municipality for comparison purposes. Obviously, you know what Tuzla is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For those of us who may not be aware, Tuzla at that point in time was a Muslim municipality in a sense, multi-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It was governed --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a predominantly Bosniak population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. That's where the army of BiH was located, and you also had HVO working along with them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And, in fact, as I understand it, the 2nd Corps of the army of BiH was located there, a rather large force, if you know? If you don't know, that's fine. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't know. I know there was something. But what, which corps, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Again, this is for comparative purposes. If we look at 1D 00854, 854, this is dated 10 July 1992. We're just going to take them in chronological order. Here, this is on mandatory payment of foreign currency, and Article 1 states: "All workers employed abroad and with permanent residence in Tuzla municipality shall make a payment of 1.000 deutschemarks for the needs of the defence of Tuzla ..." And if we look further down, we see that it's in the Privredna Banka Zagreb, and also there's another bank in Germany. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We see that at the bottom that this is signed by the president of the Presidency, a Mr. Selim Beslagic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beslagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Beslagic. Thank you very much. It would appear that, here, they're doing the same thing as in the other municipalities: Number one, sort of taxes their residence; and number two, using a non-resident account, bank account, outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. We go on to the next document, 1D 00858, 858. Again, it's dealing with Tuzla, and same gentleman has signed it. This is 30 July 1992. This is an order to pay out members of the Reconnaissance and Sabotage Platoon, and it says in the very first, Article I: "It is hereby ordered to pay out double salaries to members of the Reconnaissance and Sabotage Platoon at the recommendation of the commander of their unit." So, here, it seems that the municipality of Tuzla is also financing; and at least with this particular platoon, perhaps because of the activities they're involved in, they get to have a double salary. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We go on to the next document, 1D 00866. 866. This is dated 27 of August 1992, same gentleman, same municipality. "Decision on mandatory foreign currency payments by persons working abroad." Again, it's for comparison purposes. Now, if we look at this, we look at Article 1 and it says: "All citizens, residents of the municipality of Tuzla working abroad on a temporary basis, shall pay an amount of 2.000 deutschemarks ..." And if we look at Article 2, we see that there's a bank in Zagreb, and there's another bank that appears to be the German bank that we saw earlier, "...or with authorised agents or representatives of the municipality of Tuzla." So, again, if we look at this particular document, this decision dated 27th of August, 1992 in the municipality of Tuzla, we see, one, that they're taxing their citizens abroad -- who are working abroad; and, two, they're asking them to deposit that amount in non-residential accounts. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document, 1D 00868, 868, this is 16 September 1992. This is an order to impose special tax. If we look at the second page, we see it's the same gentleman, the president of the Presidency of Tuzla. This is a special war tax, and it says in Article II: "All legal, civil-legal entities, and natural entities involved in the sale of goods and services and the manufacture of consume products for end users in the territory of Tuzla municipality shall be liable to pay a special war tax." We see that, at least for cigarettes and alcohol, cigarettes is 30 per cent, alcohol -- cigarettes and alcohol is 30 per cent, 10 per cent on other products. So, here, we have the municipality taxing its citizens and also other entities with a special war tax, and I assume that this is all in order to finance the ABiH and other -- and for other municipal services; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me just stop before I go on to the next couple documents. Do these documents seem to be -- the activities in the documents from Tuzla, do they seem rather similar to what was happening in the various municipalities that we touched on earlier, those that were included in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, and in the whole area, as far as I know. I'm referring to the federal part, the area controlled by the BH army and controlled by the HVO. Everything was done according to the same principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we go on to the next document, 1D 01756, 1756, this is dated March 5, 1993. This is a decision. Again, if we look at the last page, again, the president of the Presidency, the same gentleman that signed the previous decisions. This one is a decision on "obligatory foreign currency payments for persons temporarily employed abroad for the year of 1993." And, if we look at Article 1, we see that there are various amounts: 2.000 deutschemarks, 1.000 deutschemarks, 500 deutschemarks. And, if we look at Article 3, if we go to Article 3, we see, again, that the payments are to be made at various non-residential -- non-residential accounts. We see, actually, in the first one, we see the Tuzla bank. So at this point, at least in Tuzla, there is a bank that's functioning. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, it was done during that period. It certainly wasn't in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. So it would appear, at least in 1993, it was possible in some places within Bosnia-Herzegovina to have banks functioning.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "functioning"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, operating.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we saw there was a bank in Mostar that was operating based on a feasibility study and a request that was made. Do you remember that yesterday we saw that and discussed that. They got permission from the central bank, the national bank of Bosnia to open up a bank account -- to open up a bank.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with that, but the functioning of a bank or operating of a bank is one of its -- one of its duties is payments with other countries. How do you imagine that the man in Tuzla or somebody in Tuzla could have payments with foreign countries, unless -- or rather, if the money -- when you send in an order, that order has to be backed up by money. So when you pay in a 100.000 marks, for example, in Germany, the person from Tuzla from the bank has to take that money physically to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So, in other words, what you're telling us is that they had the same challenges in Tuzla that they had in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far greater. Because in Mostar, well, the road was open to Croatia so you could pass by that way; whereas, Tuzla was surrounded, so they couldn't take the money out of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then we see other banks such as the one in Zagreb. We see the other bank that we talked about, the commercial bank of Mulheim Ruhr, however you pronounce it. We see another bank in Frankfurt. And you can also pay in cash at the -- at the cash desk at the Assembly of the of municipality of Tuzla. So, again, this decision is very similar to what we've seen with respect to other municipalities taxing their foreign citizens or their citizens working abroad and having them place that money in various accounts, including accounts that are outside Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with the last set of documents for this chapter, I want to go to another municipality, and this is the municipality of Maglaj. So this is the first document, 1D 00218, and this was published in the -- it says: "Pursuant to Article 42 of the decree law of defence Official Gazette of the republic of BH." It's signed by the president of the Executive Committee of the Maglaj municipality, an Ivan Grlic, and it says here: "The Natron DD joint stock company Maglaj is hereby ordered to pay travel expenses of 1.058 German marks to Ante Marincic, the commander of the HVO staff in Maglaj, incurred during the purchase of MTS material," and so on and so forth. Can you tell us anything about this gentleman or this activity or anything? Tell us, what does this order tell you at least?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this order means that -- that the technical equipment and materiel, well, you can have anything under that title. It can range from weapons, bullets, spare parts for combat, spare parts for vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if it's being paid to the commander of the HVO -- incidentally, is Maglaj municipality within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at the next document, 1D 00213, this is a decision. Again, the same gentleman signs it. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Mm-hmm. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 213. This is a decision, again based on the degree law on defence published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Maglaj municipality. It says here under Article I: "The Maglaj Municipal Secretariat for Finance is hereby ordered to make a withdrawal from the foreign currency bank account from the Maglaj Municipality Executive Council and pay 15.000 deutschemarks to the Armed Forces of Maglaj Municipality for the special procurement ..." and it goes on. And then, in Article II, it says: "The Maglaj Municipality, BH army, and HVO are obliged to present proof of the procured MTS-ammunition to the Maglaj Municipal Executive Council." Help me out here, sir. It seems that this particular municipality, which at least to your understanding is not within Herceg-Bosna, is asking for the payment or for the -- in this decision, is making a decision for a withdrawal from the foreign currency bank account. Does that mean that they have a bank account that's outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that what they're referring to when they say foreign currency bank account, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but they couldn't withdraw it anywhere else but from some non-residential account, outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I should say I'm -- it's pointed out to me that actually it's May 1993, Your Honours, as opposed to January 1993. At the preamble, it should read "May."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Now I just have -- I just want to go into one last area, and so we're going to switch gears a little bit. We talked a little bit about the assistance that was coming in from the diaspora. Do you recall that there were some questions, and you even --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You were even questioned by the Prosecutor, when you gave your statement, about that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when we're talking about money coming in from the diaspora, we saw some documents where municipalities are asking its citizens who are working abroad to make contributions. They're being taxed for the war effort. Is it fair to say -- but there were also others who were living abroad under -- that we can call the diaspora who were also donating money to the war efforts for Croatia and for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That's not a taxation. They're not being taxed. This is on a voluntary basis. They're volunteering their -- their savings to assist Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you need an example?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we're going to get there just slowly. I want to make sure I have it right. And, if I understand you correctly, some money that was being donated or being channeled to Croatia was actually earmarked for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I've been sitting quietly but I'm going to object to this, unless the witness has a personal knowledge of this. The witness was very careful in his answers to the Prosecution to only talk about things that he saw and he heard, and there were a number of times that he would not answer the Prosecution's questions because he said he did not have personal knowledge. So I'd like to have foundation for how this witness can talk about, address these matters as to whether someone somewhere in the world made a donation earmarked for Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to go step-by-step. I have no -- I have no problems with that. But just for the record, Your Honour, when the gentleman yesterday was saying that he did not have personal knowledge, I want -- I want to make sure that we're fair to the gentleman, because an allegation has been made that the gentleman was less than candid and less than truthful with the Prosecution, and that's incorrect. What the Prosecutor was attempting to do is to try to get this gentleman to commit to conversations that might have occurred where he wasn't present, and he could not state to any degree of certainty what was being said. He was very correct when he spoke to the Prosecutor in his statement, very correct when he testified under oath on direct, and he's being very correct when he's testifying here on cross. So I'll lay the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether money that was being donated to the war effort, going to Croatia, do you know whether any of that was actually being earmarked, where the donors in a sense were saying, "We wish this money to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina, or a certain percentage of it"? Do you know? "Yes, no," that will do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a yes or no answer. Yesterday, and when I talked to the Prosecution, I said that the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina paid in a large sum of money and that very little was returned to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to look at -- I want to look at one document, 1D 01755, and at least -- this is from Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And to make sure that we're fair to everyone, we realise that this particular document -- we see Mate Boban's name, but we do not see a date and we do not see a signature or a seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But if we look at it, and if we look at it closely, we talk -- in the second paragraph, it says: "All of your assistance for Bosnia and Herzegovina goes through Zagreb and our fund for the support of Croatia in Villach, Austria, which has been opened for a long period of time and is under the control of the government of the Republic of Croatia and to which you have already made your payments. You can underline on the payment slips that your contribution is intended for Bosnia and Herzegovina." I'm pausing to make sure the Prosecution reads this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It doesn't say that anyone ever did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "A defence is not something of personal character, and it does not have to do only with a village or municipality. Here we speak of the defence of Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian nation as a whole." And, then, if we go further down, it talks about, you know, Chetnik hoards. So at least we know we can sort of glean as to when this leaflet might have been printed out in any event. Assuming that this is a true and accurate document -- and I say assuming because we don't have a signature, we don't have a seal, and we don't have a date, and I want to be fair to the Prosecution because I'm constantly being attacked of being less than fair. But assuming that this is a true and accurate and complete document, does it not here say that contributions can be earmarked for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and, in fact, it gives a particular account to where that money can go to, which fund, and how to designate it for Bosnia and Herzegovina? Does it not say that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And that just confirms what I said a moment ago, that money came into the account that was controlled by the government of the Republic of Croatia and that very little was transferred to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now very quickly I want to go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, to save time, this document that has been provided by you. Where does it come from? What its origin? It looks like a letter, a circular letter sent to all those abroad, but how did you get it? The Prosecutor may have an objection to this document being admitted, so perhaps we should settle that if you have some information to provide us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The only information I can provide you, Mr. President, is that this was something that was being distributed; and through our investigation we came across in document. It's a sort of leaflet that we saw earlier. If you recall, once before, we saw a leaflet that came with the Mujahedin and how -- what they should do and how they should behave. This is the kind of leaflet that apparently -- these sort of things were being circulated at the time to provide notice to the people. That's -- so it came through our investigation. But, in due course, we will be able to tie all of this up, Your Honour, to demonstrate, to demonstrate, contrary to what the Prosecution indicates, but to demonstrate that yes, indeed, money was being earmarked for Bosnia and Herzegovina that was going through Croatian banks. So we will be able to tie this up, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 01754, just very quickly, 1754, this is a -- that is document. It's titled "Croatian national fund Chicago. Names of donors of aid to Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991, 1991, 1992, 1993." Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, if we look at this, it would seem that we have a list of names. I don't know whether you've seen this document before, but am I correct in assuming that this was a rather transparent process by which Croats from the diaspora could donate their money and there was an accounting as to who gave what, when, where, how much?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this document before, but the fact is that documents like this did exist and that they're now becoming apparent, especially in the case of General Zagorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Very good. Now if we look at the next document 1D 01753, this is just a sampling again. This is dated August 27, 1992. This is from an Ivan Nenadic, MD. "MD" stands for medical doctor. We see here that as of August 27, 1992, it's a letter. It's a letter to Mr. Mirko Volaric, president of the Croatian national association in Los Angeles, California. It's a brief summary of what they were able to achieve through south-west medical teams since September 1991. And if we just look at, for instance, on the very first page under the entry of March 15, 1992, we see that there's medical supplies, Ministry of Health, Republic of Croatia, delivered to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm raising my voice to make sure my colleague here hears me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So here we see it's going the Ministry of Health of Croatia for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Okay. Let's move on to the very last document. We can handle this before the break. This is somewhat different, but I think it might be helpful to the Trial Chamber. But just getting back to this last document, I need to ask you one question. You see where at least Mr. Nenadic is noting that in March 15, 1992, he and others were able to collect medical supplies and have them earmarked for Bosnia and Herzegovina through Croatia? You see that? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, in fact, this is not some isolated incident. This was occurring throughout the wartime?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV RUPCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now the very last document, 1D 01774, 1774. This is a -- you will see this is a letter. It's coming from the Republic of Croatia, the Ministry of Justice. It's addressed to a Mr. Karnavas. That would be me: "Subject: Mr. Jadranko Prlic, accused before ICTY-information and documents delivered." I'll read the whole part, and then I'll ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, there's an address here. It must be a public document. There's an address in Zagreb mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My particular office was closed after it was ransacked a week before trial, in the middle of the day. So anyway, that's -- we don't have to worry about the address. As far as the Ministry of Justice, I think it's a public office. So I don't see that to be a problem, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure you've understood me. It was your address.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if we look at this, we see here and I'll just read it: "Further to your letter dated --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. I apologise interrupting. But on this occasion, Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- I have to object on this point. This is a document, and I understand Mr. Karnavas has every right to prepare his Defence case. That's not -- that's not at all in question. But I submit, Your Honour, that it's not appropriate to introduce it through this witness. There is no indication that this witness has any knowledge of this document or the content of the document. This document was obviously specifically created at Mr. Karnavas's request, and he can certainly put that in in his case if he decides to put one on, and that's his choice. But this witness cannot provide any evidence about this document, and this is simply putting the Defence case in during cross-examination of a witness who has no knowledge of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President. If we look at the very -- the third paragraph of this document, it says: "Also, according to the data the Ministry of Finance has, there were no direct payments from the budget of the Republic of Croatia to BiH."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this witness cannot possibly have any personal knowledge about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I -- if I may just at least respond for the record, I'm not posing a question. Now, when I pose the question, Mr. Scott can jump up and he can object, and I'm sure I'll respond. But until such time, at least allow me the courtesy, Mr. Scott, of making my record as well. Now, there were several questions posed by Mr. Scott, and I didn't object. I didn't object. I stand here. He was trying to elicit from the gentleman, you know, answers with respect to monies that were supposedly being paid from the Republic of Croatia to Herceg-Bosna --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're entitled to ask him that question which actually is the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay if we look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the witness doesn't answer, I don't know which witness or what witness could answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is a witness, Your Honour. With all due respect, with all due respect, again, this witness comes from Mr. Muljacic from the Republic of Croatia. He is the one that prepared and made this assertion. I do object to this because this is improper. This is an improper way of introducing evidence from a third party that has no connection with this witness. If Mr. Karnavas wants to call Mr. Muljacic, or call a representative from the government of Croatia, which, which the Prosecution would then have an opportunity to cross-examine, we can do that, Your Honour. But this is just nothing more and putting in self-serving Defence evidence, and he is entitled to do that in his own case, but through this witness who has no connection to this letter or the content of the letter. It's improper, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I have settled the objections. You may put your question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This was a letter, sir, that was generated based on a request that was made during our investigative efforts to get to the truth in this case. Something that does matter to some of us. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour. Why do we have to have these constant personal remarks and attacks. There's no purpose to this. It matters to some of us. It's nothing but a snide comment. There's no reason for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 2, it says, "the agreement between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina on cooperation and mutual assistance in customs issues was signed in Sarajevo 27 July 2000, which means that the Ministry of Finances does not have the documentation on cooperation with the customs service of BiH in the period 1991-1994." It thence goes on to say, based on certain questions that were being asked as part of our investigative efforts to get to documentation that might help had us get to the truth: "Also, according to the data the Ministry of Finance has, there were no direct payments from the budget of the Republic of Croatia to BiH." Can you comment on this? If you can't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before he answers the question, I want to know what's his personal -- what is his foundation to have knowledge? Before he answers and voices an opinion, I want the witness to be asked: Do you have any personal knowledge of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we get there, first, it's can he answer the question. Yes or no? If it's yes, then I can go that one next step.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I appreciate Mr. Scott's assistance in teaching me how to lay a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I don't approve of the way with which you work. In the indictment, the accused are being charged with joint criminal enterprise on funding coming from the Republic of Croatia. The Defence is trying to come up with data that contradicts what you have said. Defence counsel is putting questions. The Ministry of Justice is answering, and says in second paragraph that they have no documents from 1991 to 1994. But in the third paragraph, the Ministry of Justice states that according to the Ministry of Finance, there have been no direct payments from the budget of the Republic of Croatia to the BiH. The witness is a witness who has been in charge of financial matters, who was a deputy minister. He may have an opinion and may have something to say about such a document. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I have to strenuously object. The Chamber doesn't understand nature of my objection. My objection is not that the Defence does not have the right to put on such evidence in a proper way. If, if we were in the Defence case, if we were in the Defence case and Mr. Karnavas wanted to tender this document to the Court, he would have to put it in through a -- he couldn't just say, "Your Honour, I tender a letter from Mr. Muljacic, and I think it's very important." He would have to produce a witness who could come into court and be subject to cross-examination about such a letter. You would not allow him in the Defence case to simply tender this document with no foundation and no witness. You wouldn't allow that, but now you're going to allow him -- you're allowing him to do it through a witness who has no connection to this document at all and no basis for it,, the witness was, again, very careful yesterday. The Chamber may recall, and Your Honour, Mr. President, you characterised this witness yesterday as essentially a courier. He was essentially a courier. That was the President's, your own words. Then he says, "I don't want to take about anything I didn't see other hear himself." Here, we're going to ask him to voice an opinion on a letter from the assistant minister in Croatia. I strenuously object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may be heard and perhaps we could just cool the temperature in the room a little bit. The Prosecution in direct examination was trying to elicit very specific information from this particular witness. At the time, the Prosecution was very confident in posing those sorts of questions and expecting the sorts of answers that I guess he hoped to get. At that point in time, the witness, obviously to the Prosecution, seemed competent to answer those questions. The witness occasionally said that he was a courier. That was primarily what his function was, but nonetheless he was pressed. And when the gentleman was unable to answer some of the rather direct questions that the Prosecution was posing, then the Prosecution's tactic changed. At that point in time, the witness became, although not claimed to be hostile, became in a sense a hostile witness and was treated as such, not merely in the form of the questioning, but also in the tone of the questioning. Now, as you've indicated, Mr. President, the gentleman here has dealt with financial matters. At this point in time, I'm merely asking a question whether he knows. We haven't heard the answer. If he doesn't know, I sit down. If he knows, I ask him how do you know? He explains. If it's sufficient, I move on and press forward. Also, might I remind the Prosecution that, in the Defence case, assuming there is one, I'm also to avail myself of the very same tactics that the Prosecution does; in other words, introduce documents without any viva voce testimony, or any foundation, for that matter. The Prosecution does it routinely. I'm merely asking one simple question. It is not a self-serving document either. This was based on a request made. It was a formal request. We got an answer. So it's not something I asked from this gentleman, who incidentally is a diplomat, an ambassador right now. I didn't ask him to help the Defence in any personal matter. This was an official of the government of the Republic of Croatia, and he has an obligation to help because he works on the Office of Cooperation. It's through that office that we make formal requests. This was an investigative effort, and I don't see why the Prosecutor is getting all excited. I simply do not understand. What have I done to the Prosecutor today?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I am excited because this is an entirely improper way to introduce this sort of evidence, Your Honour. Yes. I am excited because this is entirely improper. It's entirely improper, and it's not the same as what the -- you know, Karnavas's ploy is, you know, a best defence is a good offence, and he turns around and he attacks the Prosecution every time. This was a document prepared specifically at the request of the Defence team by Mr. Muljacic or someone. Mr. Muljacic should be required to come into court and defend what he says in this statement, not getting it in, sneaking this document in through a witness who doesn't know anything about it. This is entirely improper. It has nothing to do with anything the Prosecution has done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Just by way of example, Mr. President, just very quickly; then we can take the break and we can decide what to do. Earlier, I referred to a document, Prosecution document P 00985. That was the document that was in the particular motion that I indicated that we need to respond to. That was the document that was not fully translated, and it was not in the bundle. This is the sort of same document, same type of document that the Prosecution is now using through its motions. Nobody's coming in to testify about these documents. No foundation is laid, nothing, but the Prosecution seems to think that that's okay. Now I'm learning from the Prosecutor. He's teaching me these techniques. I'm doing exactly what they're doing, and I'm grateful for his -- for his teaching.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You need to remain calm, Mr. Karnavas. Witness, the problem is as follows: We have before us a document that seems to be saying that, according to the Republic of Croatia, there was no funding from the budget made available to the ABiH [as interpreted]. Even if you were a courier, you did indicate that you worked in the finance department. Perhaps you know nothing about it. In that case, we can leave it at that.
